title: Randy Lubin & Raph D'Amico - Dungeon Court
speaker: Randy Lubin & Raph D'Amico
summary: Randy Lubin and Raph D'Amico run the debut of Dungeon Court, a live audience LARP adapted from Jason Morningstar's Ghost Court (Bully Pulpit Games), framed as Judge Judy for dungeon monsters and heroes. They pick a setting with Azgaar's fantasy map generator, then audience members play randomly drawn monster and hero characters in short scripted-premise cases before rotating judges (an arch-lich, then a city magistrate). The cases riff on roguelike tropes: dungeon hazards as workplace safety, riddle-asking guards, a mandatory shop per level, unidentified potions that turn an ally into a rat, and an undead neighbour. It is a performance with little explicit design commentary; the few insights concern its structure as a light improv game.

insights.claim: Dungeon Court adapts Bully Pulpit Games' Ghost Court, a Judge Judy-style comedic court game, into a live LARP where audience members argue ridiculous cases between monsters and heroes.
insights.detail: Lubin describes Ghost Court as Judge Judy with ghosts, telling ridiculous cases between ghosts and humans. Dungeon Court reskins it with monster-versus-monster, human-versus-monster and human-versus-human cases across a dungeon, a city and a temple.
insights.quote: it is Judge Judy but with ghosts where you tell a series of very ridiculous cases between ghosts and humans

insights.claim: Dungeon Court keeps cases short and structured: the plaintiff gets one minute, the defendant one minute, and the judge about three minutes to question, rule and sentence.
insights.detail: While one case plays on stage, the next volunteers are set up offstage by Raph, so cases run back to back.
insights.quote: the plaintiff is going to have one minute to state their case the defendant is then gonna have one minute to respond

insights.claim: Dungeon Court randomly pairs plaintiffs and defendants from a printed deck of monsters and heroes with pre-written cases, each player getting a card describing their side.
insights.detail: Each card gives a short case description from one side and the drawn character gives traits (e.g. a smelly, gregarious blob or a voracious, miserly swamp worm). Lubin says this gives players scaffolding so they don't come to the case cold.
insights.quote: we're giving you some scaffolding you're not coming to these cases

insights.claim: To set Dungeon Court's scene in the spirit of the event, the hosts randomly generated a world with Azgaar's fantasy map generator and zoomed in to pick a border region and city.
insights.detail: They chose a fraught border region and foothills likely to hold ancient dungeons as the locale, then invented the 'Dungeon of Infinite Depths', which actually only has 26 depths.
insights.quote: we're gonna use as gars fantasy map generator or they think this is very much in the spirit of roguelike celebration

insights.claim: A Dungeon Court case dramatizes the roguelike trope of handing an ally an unidentified potion, which polymorphed her into a rat that could not carry her treasure.
insights.detail: The wizard defendant argued an unidentified potion could well have been useful; the judge ordered that for the next five unidentified potions they find, they split and both drink them to share the consequences.
insights.quote: for the next five times and the two of you encounter a potion of a dungeon you must split it equally into two bottles
